newsitem.title: GREECE: GREEK BOND MARKET NEEDS INFRASTRUCTURE- BANKER.
newsitem.headline: GREEK BOND MARKET NEEDS INFRASTRUCTURE- BANKER.

text.p: Greece's bond market has made important strides in the last few years but it still lacks a fully developed institutional infrastructure, said George Georgiou, general manager at Bayerische Vereinsbank- Athens.
"The Greek capital markets have seen strong growth during the latter part of the 1980s and the begining of the 1990s with government securities dominating the market," he said.
Georgiou was speaking at a Euromoney conference titled "Greece: A new role in regional and international markets.
The significant divergence of Athens stock exchange bond prices used for documentary portfolio valuation from real market prices raised questions about the reliability of present valuations, he said.
The lack of institutional infrastructure might discourage investors from actively participating in drachma bond trading, Georgiou said.
Bond trading on the Athens stock exchange has been very thin, prompting players to question whether quoted prices are fair.
The introduction of a generic secondary system of market makers for bonds with prices quoted on Reuters screens enhanced the efficiency and liquidity of the over-the-counter market, he added.
"The planned introduction of a full-scale primary and secondary market electronic system by the Bank of Greece at the end of 1997, will hopefully address this matter," said Georgiou.

Although issues related to the reimbursement of the withholding tax on government securities for qualified non-residents had been fully clarified, there were lingering questions about domestic investors, he added.
Joining the chorus of bankers who have called for the auctioning of the 12-month T-Bill, which is the benchmark rate for FRNs, Georgiou said administratively set rates created unwarranted basis risk.

Rates on 12-month T-bills, currently at a gross rate of 9.60 percent, are usually set by the finance ministry. The treasury imposes a 7.5 percent withholding tax on interest income from state securities.
"The introduction of a domestic derivatives market, especially for much needed instruments such as interest rate futures, will provide hedging strategies to investors," Georgiou told the conference.

Greece's adherence to the EU-approved convergence plan, the substantial narrowing of spreads due to recent credit upgrades and a zero-risk weight for Hellenic Republic holdings made drachma denominated securities more attractive to foreign investors, he added.

Moody's Investor Services upgraded Greece's long-term sovereign foreign currency debt to Baa1 from Baa3 in late 1996 and IBCA, the European credit agency, to BBB from BBB-. -- Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
